strengths: Novel exact characterization of NSR for linear-quadratic and polynomial systems using lifted dynamics and Isserlis theorem
Rigorous mathematical treatment with complete proofs and sophisticated variance decompositions
Concrete mechanistic explanation for training instabilities: NSR diverges as optimal deterministic policy is approached (Corollary 6)
Clear progression from simple (one-step LQG, Theorem 3) to complex (multi-step, polynomial, nonlinear) systems
Effective visualization of NSR landscapes with optimizer trajectories validating theoretical predictions
Upper bounds provided for general nonlinear dynamics (Theorem 10)
Comprehensive appendix with detailed proofs supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Exact results limited to linear and polynomial systems; most modern RL uses neural networks in complex nonlinear environments with vastly different properties
Bounds for general nonlinear case (Theorem 10) are loose, with undefined constant C in Eq. 25 and limited insight into neural network behavior
Restriction to vanilla REINFORCE without variance reduction (baselines, GAE) severely limits practical relevance; these techniques are standard precisely because they address variance
Paper diagnoses NSR divergence problem but proposes no solutions; future work section mentions variance reduction but develops nothing concrete
Experimental validation only on toy problems (double integrator, pendulum) with short horizons (T≤30); no realistic environments or deep neural networks
Computational complexity exponential in horizon T and combinatorial in polynomial degree; practical computability for realistic systems unaddressed
Finite-horizon assumption and Gaussian diagonal-covariance policies are restrictive

strengths: Rigorous mathematical development with exact closed-form NSR characterizations for linear and polynomial systems using sophisticated techniques (Gaussian moments, lifted dynamics)
Systematic progression from one-step LQG through multi-step linear, polynomial, to general nonlinear systems demonstrates thorough theoretical scope
Derivation of interpretable scaling laws (e.g., NSR ~ (σ₀/σ)⁶) provides intuition for how NSR depends on exploration and initial state uncertainty
Empirical validation across multiple system classes (double integrator, polynomial, LQR/Pendulum with MLP) shows theoretical predictions broadly align with numerical results
Careful attention to mathematical detail in proofs, including parity analysis, moment expansions, and handling of conditional expectations
weaknesses: Severely limited practical relevance: exact characterizations only apply to linear/polynomial systems; for neural policies (most practical case), only loose upper bounds are available (Theorem 10) involving unknown quantities like E[R(τ)⁴] and ‖Jθ(st)‖, making them uninformative

Restrictive problem setting: linear Gaussian policies with diagonal covariance, finite-horizon episodic setting, no function approximation error, no treatment of modern methods (actor-critic, PPO, TRPO), limiting generalization

Limited conceptual novelty: the core finding (high variance near optima as σ → 0) is expected from basic variance scaling; Corollary 6 (optimal policies are deterministic) is obvious in the LQG setting; characterizes known phenomenon rather than enabling new understanding

No algorithmic contributions: paper identifies the problem but offers no concrete solutions beyond suggesting 'variance reduction techniques' should be designed; doesn't demonstrate that NSR understanding actually improves algorithms compared to existing methods

Weak connection between theory and empirics: NSR increase near optimality is documented but causality with optimization instability is correlational not proven; Figure 4 shows policy collapse correlated with NSR spike but relationship is unclear

Insufficient experimental validation: restricted to toy problems (2D double integrator, T≤6 polynomial horizons, classic control); no comparison with variance reduction methods (GAE, baselines); no ablations on design choices; Figure 6 (MLP) uses expensive Monte Carlo NSR estimation without demonstrating algorithmic improvement

Technical concerns with generalization: Theorem 7 bounds depend on ‖FS‖²₂ ~ ρ(F)^(2T), exponential in horizon for unstable systems, making bounds vacuous; Proposition 9 complexity is exponential in degree and horizon; Theorem 10's constant C unspecified and Jacobian-dependent (problematic for bang-bang controllers)

Missing critical comparisons: insufficient contrast with Preiss et al. (2019) on what's fundamentally new; no comparison of NSR reduction under different variance reduction techniques; limited engagement with recent literature on policy collapse and training instability mechanisms

Presentation issues: dense technical sections with Isserlis expansions buried in main text; main insights obscured by mathematical details; figure captions lack sufficient explanation; notation (M̄ss, IS_Ω) introduced without sufficient motivation

strengths: Novel characterization of noise-to-signal ratio landscape showing NSR increases near policy optimality, providing concrete mechanism for understanding training instability

Strong theoretical contributions: exact closed-form NSR expressions for linear systems (Theorem 3), exact computational procedures for multi-step LQG via lifted dynamics (Theorems 5&7), bounds for general nonlinear systems (Theorem 10)

Clear practical insights: NSR scales as σ⁻² when policy becomes deterministic (Σ→0), exponential variance growth with horizon when closed-loop system is unstable, explicit dependence on initial-state and policy covariance
Rigorous mathematical treatment using Gaussian moment evaluation (Isserlis theorem) and elegant lifted-dynamics reduction; proofs appear sound and complete
Comprehensive experimental validation across linear, polynomial, and neural network systems with clear visualization of NSR landscapes and optimization trajectories
Well-organized presentation with logical progression from simple (one-step) to complex (nonlinear) systems, making insights accessible despite dense mathematics
weaknesses: Severely limited practical scope: restriction to vanilla REINFORCE without baselines critically limits relevance—baselines are essential in practice and fundamentally change variance structure, making analysis of baseline-free REINFORCE of limited applicability

Exact characterizations have limited practical utility: Theorem 3 restricted to one-step systems; Theorem 5's exact expressions are extremely complex (six-term decomposition) without significant intuitive value beyond simpler bounds in Theorem 7; exact computation is expensive and impractical

Upper bounds for nonlinear systems (Theorem 10) lack tightness analysis—no validation of bound quality shown; Figure 6 uses Monte Carlo estimation rather than theoretical bounds, providing no empirical validation of bound tightness

Restrictive problem setting limits generality: finite-horizon only (infinite-horizon discounted problems are standard in RL); Gaussian policies with diagonal covariance only; no analysis of state-value or other baselines; no consideration of entropy regularization where optimal policies are stochastic

Primarily diagnostic rather than prescriptive: paper identifies high-NSR regions but provides no concrete solutions or variance-reduction techniques; conclusion mentions solution design as future work

Insufficient investigation of optimization dynamics: Figure 2 shows SGD/Adam oscillate near optimum but mechanism is not analyzed—sensitivity to learning rate, batch size, momentum parameters unexplored

Limited experimental scope: most experiments on toy systems (double integrator, quadratic/cubic dynamics); neural network experiments only on LQR and Pendulum; no evaluation on realistic high-dimensional continuous control or complex RL benchmarks

Incomplete comparison to prior work: acknowledges Preiss et al. (2019) but provides no direct empirical comparison showing improvements; positioning relative to prior variance analyses could be stronger
Corollary 6 (deterministic optimal policy) is specific to LQR-type cost structures; generality for other reward structures (risk-sensitive, stochastic environments) unclear and not discussed

strengths: Exact closed-form NSR characterizations for linear-quadratic systems (Theorem 3) and polynomial systems via moment evaluation (Proposition 10) are non-trivial theoretical contributions with careful mathematical treatment.
Key insight that NSR diverges as policies approach optimality (due to Σ→0) provides a unifying explanation for training instability and connects to the exploration-exploitation tradeoff.
Comprehensive progression from one-step to multi-step LQG with lifted dynamics (Theorems 5-6), and extension to nonlinear systems with upper bounds (Theorem 11).

Careful experimental validation across multiple problem classes: linear systems, polynomial systems, and nonlinear systems with neural policies, including detailed ablation studies (Figure 7) isolating statistical error.

Clear empirical demonstration (Figures 2, 4-6) that NSR growth correlates with training instability (oscillations in SGD/Adam but not GD), with coherent mechanism explained by deterministic optimal policies.
Rigorous technical execution using Isserlis' theorem, Gaussian moment calculus, and lifted dynamics with detailed proofs in appendices.
weaknesses: Scope of exact characterizations severely limited: theory only applies to linear/polynomial systems with Gaussian diagonal policies. For practical deep RL with neural networks, only loose upper bounds via Theorem 11 are available, with no analysis of bound tightness.

Theory-practice gap: Figure 6 (most realistic experiments) relies on Monte Carlo NSR estimation, which defeats the main value proposition of exact characterizations. Loose bounds may not be predictive for neural network policies.

Limited actionability: paper identifies NSR as a problem but provides no algorithmic solutions or design principles. Discussions of baselines and entropy regularization (Section 5) are speculative without empirical validation that they solve the NSR issue.

Incomplete optimization analysis: Theorem 4 only shows escape is *possible* (not typical or frequent), requires unverified condition on noise, and lacks convergence analysis connecting NSR growth to actual sample or iteration complexity.

Experimental limitations: linear/polynomial experiments are toy problems (2D double integrator, T≤6 horizons); MuJoCo experiments only in appendix relying on Monte Carlo NSR. Missing comparisons: no experiments validating that variance-reduction methods mitigate NSR issues.

Theorem 8 provides only upper bounds (not exact characterization like Theorem 6), weakening the multi-step contribution. Analysis uses restrictive isotropic assumptions (Σ=σ²I) not always satisfied in practice.
No comparison with Preiss et al. (2019) on what is genuinely new beyond existing variance characterizations for LQG. Limited discussion of relationship to sample complexity and problem conditioning.

strengths: Technically sound mathematical analysis with elegant use of lifted dynamics and Isserlis theorem for exact moment computations
Clear scaling laws (e.g., NSR ∝ σ₀⁶/σ²) provide interpretable dependence on policy and initial-state covariance
Well-structured progression from one-step to multi-step to polynomial systems with both theory and verification
Explicit connection between gradient-estimator statistics and escape dynamics through Theorem 4
weaknesses: Exact characterizations limited to linear and polynomial systems; for realistic neural network policies (Figure 6), resorts to Monte Carlo estimation that the paper acknowledges fails to capture trends, undermining the core value proposition

Insights are largely confirmatory rather than novel: policy variance collapse causing instability is well-known; the optimal policy being deterministic is trivial; NSR increasing near optimality follows from small gradient norms

Theorem 4 (escape from fixed ball) is weak—provides only positive probability of escape, not typical convergence failure; gap between escaping a ball and practical training instability is loosely motivated
NSR metric choice questionable: normalizing by ||∇J||² artificially inflates NSR when gradient is small near suboptimal points; why not coefficient of variation or other robust metrics?

Experiments predominantly on toy problems (double integrator, polynomial systems); Figure 4 uses unrealistic hyperparameters (batch size 64, learning rate 10⁻²); MuJoCo experiments only show correlation, not causation; no comparison with standard stabilization methods (PPO, TRPO, SAC)
Significant gap between theory and practice: paper provides no new algorithmic solutions—recommendations are well-established (entropy regularization, baselines, variance reduction techniques)
Upper bounds (Theorem 8 for multi-step, Theorem 11 for nonlinear) merely confirm intuitive scaling without providing convergence guarantees, convergence rates, or actionable guidance
Dense mathematical exposition obscures practical insights; unclear take-home message for practitioners or algorithm designers; no discussion of when analysis fails or provides pessimistic predictions

strengths: Novel NSR perspective that naturally captures relative informativeness of gradient estimates, connecting estimator quality to optimization behavior in a way that differs meaningfully from prior variance-focused analyses
Rigorous exact characterizations for linear systems (Theorem 3) and multi-step LQG systems (Theorems 5-6) via elegant use of lifted dynamics and moment-evaluation algorithms with Isserlis theorem

Fundamental theoretical insight: Corollary 7 reveals that optimal policies in LQG must be deterministic, making NSR divergence inevitable at optimality—this identifies a deep exploration-exploitation tension inherent to REINFORCE
Excellent experimental validation across multiple system classes with effective NSR landscape visualizations and optimization trajectory overlays showing NSR increases near optimality
Convincing ablation studies (Figure 7) demonstrating policy collapse is caused by statistical error: larger batch sizes delay collapse, exact gradients prevent it entirely
Clear technical progression from one-step to multi-step linear systems to polynomial systems to general nonlinear dynamics, with each stage building systematically
Theorem 4 connects variance blow-up to probabilistic escape from bounded optimization regions, and Theorem 9 characterizes how horizon and closed-loop stability affect variance growth
Proper treatment of technical depth and limitations, including complexity analysis of moment-evaluation and discussion of when results apply
weaknesses: Exact NSR characterizations restricted to linear and polynomial systems; for neural network policies on nonlinear dynamics, only upper bounds are provided (Theorem 11) with unclear tightness

No algorithmic contributions or practical remedies proposed despite identifying a significant problem; discussions of baselines and entropy regularization acknowledge they don't solve the fundamental NSR divergence issue
Restrictive assumptions limit applicability: diagonal covariance Gaussian policies only, linear or polynomial feedback required, finite-horizon episodic setting; most practical deep RL violates these

Critical gap between theory and practice: Monte Carlo NSR estimation fails even with substantial rollout budgets (Appendix B), making it unclear how practitioners should use these insights in practice

Experimental validation primarily on toy/small-scale problems (2D integrator, polynomial systems, Pendulum); MuJoCo experiments only show empirical NSR-objective coupling without systematic algorithmic comparisons

Results problem-specific: Corollary 7 and NSR divergence mechanism apply only to settings with deterministic optimal policies; stochastic optimal policies (common in many problems) not addressed
